newsitem.title: VIRGIN ISLANDS: US Virgin Islands leaders pledge to resolve status.
newsitem.headline: US Virgin Islands leaders pledge to resolve status.

text.p: Political status, a hot topic in neighboring Puerto Rico, is quietly moving to the front burner in the U.S. Virgin Islands, after years in which the issue hardly made a ripple in public debate.

At a Senate session this week, Sen. Lorraine Berry, president of the legislature and co-chairman of the Virgin Islands Commission on Status and Federal Relations, pledged that she would make the islands' status a priority.

"Under my administration, status will be an important issue," she said. Berry noted movement in the U.S. Congress toward tackling the political status of Puerto Rico and Guam, the Pacific Ocean territory, and said, "Once that gets settled in Washington, they will be looking at us."
At issue is whether the Virgin Islands, which the United States purchased from Denmark in 1917, should remain a U.S. territory, seek statehood or push for independence.

Currently, the Virgin Islands is an unincorporated U.S. territory with a delegate, but no representative, in the House of Representatives. People born in the islands are U.S. citizens, but do not vote in presidential elections.

Known principally as a tourist destination -- the main islands of St. Thomas, St. John and St. Croix host 2 million visitors per year -- the Virgin Islands lie about 70 miles (113 km) east of Puerto Rico bordering the Caribbean Sea.

They have a total population of about 121,000, and a fairly high standard of living, although a series of bad hurricanes, drop in tourism and run of business closings and layoffs have slowed the islands' economy.

Virgin Islands Gov. Roy Schneider Thursday asked Congress for authority to seek short-term loans to cover payrolls and other government expenses. The government owes more than $1 billion in income tax refunds, payments to vendors and retroactive wages.
Schneider said that once the territory's economy was on an even keel, its residents needed to think about better defining the islands' relationship with the U.S. mainland.

"It is indeed the position of the majority of persons in the territory, that when the economic picture is better, the time would be right to pursue the enactment of a new constitution and a change in our status," he said.

Besides tourism, the island's economy relies on a giant Hess oil refinery on St. Croix and manufacturing plants set up by U.S. companies taking advantage of tax breaks offered to promote investment in the territory.

The Virgin Islands government has had a Status Commission since 1988. But a referendum vote in October 1993 drew only a 31.4 percent turnout. Of the 10,732 ballots cast, 80 percent favored continued territorial status, 13 percent backed integration with the United States and just 5 percent, or 528 people, said they backed removing U.S. sovereignty.
The other 2 percent of ballots were blank or spoiled.
A second referendum to more tightly define the status options would have been held if a majority of voters turned out, but the turnout sent the issue from the public mind.

"We need to begin an education process," said Donna Christian Green, the Virgin Islands' delegate to the U.S. Congress. "We need to develop a self-sufficiency within the territory so that when we have to decide, or when we are called on to decide, we can be in a position to make choices."
But educating the public to think about an obscure political topic could be a big job, given a focus on pocketbook issues or enjoying the islands' beaches.
